sections.h2: What an affidavit of heirship does in Texas
sections.html:
An affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement about who a dead person's relatives were, recorded in the county deed records so that later readers of the title can see it. It records facts. It does not hand title to anyone by itself.

Estates Code Sec. 203.001 gives the document a specific evidentiary job. A court must treat a recorded statement of family history, marital status or the identity of heirs as prima facie evidence when it sits in a properly sworn or acknowledged instrument and has been of record for five years or more. The five years run in the deed records of the county where the land sits, or of the county where the decedent lived. If the statement has an error, anyone interested can prove the true facts, and the affidavit does not cut off an omitted heir or a creditor.

For a seller, the buyer's side decides whether it trusts the affidavit. It is a sworn statement that no court has verified, and no law forces a third party to accept it.

Section 203.002 prints a model form, and an affidavit that follows it substantially is the safest starting point. The form asks the person signing to describe how they know the family and then to list facts in numbered paragraphs.

  • Who the affiant is, where they live, and how long they knew the decedent.
  • The decedent's date and place of death and last residence.
  • The decedent's marital history, with the date and place of a spouse's death if the spouse died first.
  • Each child, with birth date, the other parent and current address, or the date of death and descendants of a child who died.
  • Whether the decedent had a will, whether any administration took place, and whether debts or estate taxes remain unpaid.
  • The real property the decedent owned an interest in, to the best of the affiant's knowledge.

The form closes with a signature and a notary's jurat. Paragraphs for parents and siblings apply only when no descendants survived, so the right version depends on the family. A title company reading the affidavit will look for gaps in the children paragraph first, because an unlisted child is the classic way these documents fail.

sections.h2: Who inherits when there is no will
sections.html:
Estates Code ch. 201 sets the order. The affidavit has to match this order, so read the rules before anyone signs.

With no spouse, the estate goes to children and their descendants. If no child line survives, it goes in equal shares to the father and mother, and then to siblings and their descendants when a parent is gone. With a surviving spouse, the statute splits the estate into separate property and community property. The community estate passes entirely to the surviving spouse when the decedent left no descendants, or when every surviving child is also the spouse's child. If a child of another relationship survives, the decedent's undivided half of the community passes to that child line.

Separate real estate follows a different formula. With children, the spouse takes a life estate in one-third of the land and the children take the remainder. With no children, the spouse takes half of the land outright and the rest passes under the descent rules. These splits are why a house owned by a long-married couple can produce an affidavit very different from a house the decedent owned before marriage.

sections.h2: Is an affidavit enough to close a sale?
sections.html:
Sometimes, but the outcome rests on the buyer and the title company, not on the statute. The affidavit proves family facts. A title insurer still has to accept those facts and insure the buyer against a missing heir.

Section 201.053 offers protection that matters here. A buyer who pays value and relies in good faith on an affidavit that omits a child who was not a presumed child, and who has no knowledge of that child's claim, still gets good title to the interest. The omitted child can pursue the heirs for sale proceeds, so the risk shifts to the family rather than the purchaser. Ownership claims by undisclosed or missing heirs count as title defects, which explains why insurers scrutinize these papers.

Expect a title company to ask for a recorded affidavit, a death certificate, and often a signature from every heir at closing. If anyone refuses, or if the heirs cannot be located, a court-based route is usually cleaner.

sections.h2: Other ways to clear title to inherited property
sections.html:
Several routes exist, and the right choice turns on whether a will exists, whether debts need handling, and whether anyone contests who the heirs are.

Routes for passing a Texas decedent's real property
RouteCourt order neededDocument filed with the clerk
Affidavit of heirshipNoSworn affidavit in the deed records
Muniment of titleYesCourt order and the will
Administered estateYesExecutor's or administrator's deed
Transfer on death deedNoDeed filed before death, then an affidavit of death and the death certificate
Determination of heirshipYesCourt judgment naming the heirs

A clerk cannot add heirs to the old deed afterward, so choose the route before the listing goes live.

sections.h2: Property tax and homestead after a death
sections.html:
The tax bill keeps coming, and the heirs must deal with it. Bills become delinquent on a set schedule with penalties, so ask the county tax office for the dates.

Heirs living in the house may also qualify for an exemption. Anyone not named on a recorded deed must give the appraisal district a sworn statement of ownership interest, the death certificate, a recent utility bill and any court record citation. A recorded heirship affidavit can support the ownership paperwork.

Get the current balance from the county tax assessor-collector before accepting an offer.

Basis for inherited property comes from Publication 551 rather than from the purchase price, so heirs should pull that publication before they compute any gain. Basis normally means cost, but property acquired by gift or inheritance follows separate rules.

If the house sells, Form 1099-S may be issued, and a sale must be reported when you receive that form even if the gain is excludable. Texas has no state income tax. A CPA can tell you how basis, holding period and the home-sale exclusion apply to your particular heirs.

A cash sale lets the heirs close without waiting on a buyer's loan approval, which helps when several relatives live in different places and must each sign.

faqs.q: Is a Texas affidavit of heirship the same as a deed?
faqs.a: No. A deed conveys title. An affidavit states family facts and is recorded in the county deed records. Under Estates Code Sec. 203.001 it becomes prima facie evidence in court after five years of record, but it does not transfer ownership.

faqs.q: Who can sign an affidavit of heirship?
faqs.a: The statutory form calls for an affiant with personal knowledge of the decedent's family and marital history, signing before a notary. The form's optional paragraph also lets the affiant name others who know the family. Title companies often prefer someone who is not an heir.

faqs.q: Does a title company have to accept one?
faqs.a: No. Nothing in the law forces a third party to accept it. Whether a title insurer will cover a buyer depends on how complete the affidavit looks and whether any heir is missing or disputes the facts.

faqs.q: What if the affidavit leaves out a child?
faqs.a: A good-faith buyer who pays value and does not know of the child's claim can keep good title under Estates Code Sec. 201.053, but the omitted child may pursue the heirs for sale proceeds. The error can also delay a closing while the title company sorts it out.

At the county clerk's office, which keeps the deed records for the property's county. An instrument must be signed and acknowledged or sworn before an authorized officer. Ask the clerk for current fees.
